items.followUp: How can deforestation affect the water table?

rubric.why: Shows that eucalyptus uses large quantities of water.
rubric.description: Eucalyptus absorbs and loses large quantities of water through transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that eucalyptus has a high water demand or transpiration rate.

rubric.why: Connects this water use to the effect on the water table.
rubric.description: Its heavy water use can lower or deplete the water table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the lowering or depletion of the water table.

modelAnswer: Eucalyptus plants use large quantities of water and lose much of it through transpiration.
This can lower or deplete the water table.

items.followUp: Why can excessive pumping of groundwater lower the water table?

rubric.why: Identifies the first two stages of karyokinesis in sequence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming prophase and metaphase in the correct sequence.

rubric.why: Identifies the last two stages of karyokinesis in sequence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming anaphase and telophase in the correct sequence.

modelAnswer: The phases of karyokinesis, in sequence, are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.

items.followUp: Name two events during meiosis that lead to genetic variation.

rubric.why: Identifies the exchange of genetic material as a source of variation.
rubric.description: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes produces new gene combinations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning crossing over and its role in producing new combinations.

rubric.why: Identifies the random distribution of chromosomes as another source of variation.
rubric.description: Independent assortment of chromosomes produces different combinations in gametes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning independent or random assortment of chromosomes.

modelAnswer: During meiosis, crossing over between homologous chromosomes creates new combinations of genes.
Independent assortment of chromosomes also produces different combinations in gametes, causing variation in the next generation.

items.followUp: What is aerobic respiration, and name its two main stages.

rubric.why: Defines fermentation as the breakdown of glucose without oxygen.
rubric.description: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to release energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down without oxygen; mention of energy is also acceptable.

rubric.why: Names the two types of fermentation.
rubric.description: The two types are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both types.

modelAnswer: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to release energy.
Its two types are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

items.followUp: How does temperature affect enzyme activity? Give an example.

rubric.why: States that enzymes have a pH at which their activity is greatest.
rubric.description: Each enzyme works best at an optimum pH.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that enzyme activity is maximum at its optimum pH.

rubric.why: Provides a suitable example linking an enzyme to its pH conditions.
rubric.description: For example, pepsin works best in acidic conditions; trypsin works best in alkaline conditions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct enzyme and corresponding pH condition.

modelAnswer: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works best; a pH that is too high or too low reduces its activity.
For example, pepsin works best in acidic conditions.

items.followUp: What is a substrate, and how does it interact with an enzyme?

rubric.why: Identifies the active site as a specific part of an enzyme.
rubric.description: The active site is a particular region of an enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as a region or part of an enzyme.

rubric.why: Explains the active site's role in substrate binding or catalysis.
rubric.description: The substrate binds to the active site, where the reaction is catalysed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate binds or fits there, or that the reaction occurs there.

modelAnswer: The active site is the particular region of an enzyme where the substrate binds.
The reaction is catalysed at the active site.

items.followUp: What is the role of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?

rubric.description: Bile is a digestive fluid produced by the liver.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying bile as a fluid produced or secreted by the liver.

rubric.why: Gives a correct function of bile.
rubric.description: Bile emulsifies fats and helps neutralize acidic chyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either emulsifying fats or neutralizing acidic chyme.

modelAnswer: Bile is a digestive fluid produced by the liver.
It emulsifies fats and helps neutralize acidic chyme entering the small intestine.

items.followUp: How do digestion and absorption differ?

rubric.why: Describes the bolus and where or how it forms.
rubric.description: A bolus is chewed food mixed with saliva in the mouth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying bolus as food mixed with saliva or chewed food in the mouth.

rubric.why: Describes the chyme and where or how it forms.
rubric.description: Chyme is partially digested food mixed with gastric juice in the stomach.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying chyme as food mixed with gastric juice or partially digested food in the stomach.

modelAnswer: A bolus is chewed food mixed with saliva in the mouth.
Chyme is partially digested food mixed with gastric juice in the stomach.
